answer_text:
Switching to the metric system in the US would be an **enormously difficult** undertaking — not impossible, but incredibly complex. Here's a breakdown of the major challenges and considerations:

---

## 🏗️ Infrastructure Costs

Every speed limit sign across the nation would have to be changed from miles per hour to kilometers per hour — on every city street, country road, and freeway. And that's just one example. The US retains its customary system primarily due to the immense economic costs of converting industrial, manufacturing, and transportation infrastructure. Deep-rooted familiarity, a lack of mandatory federal adoption, and the logistical challenge of replacing billions of dollars' worth of equipment make the transition impractical.

---

## 💰 Financial Cost

Canada went metric back in 1970, and it took about 15 years and more than $1 billion to update everything. The US is a much larger country, so the cost would be far greater. In 2015, NASA estimated that a total conversion to the metric system would cost them $370 million alone — though sixteen years earlier, they lost $125 million when the Mars Climate Orbiter crashed due to a confusion over units.

---

## 🏭 Industrial & Manufacturing Legacy

When the Industrial Revolution began in the US, expensive manufacturing plants became a main source of American jobs and consumer products. Because the Imperial System was in place at this time, the machinery used in these factories was developed to size in Imperial units, all of the workers were trained to deal with Imperial units, and many products were made to feature Imperial units.

Today, with mass production of goods, switching everything over to a new measurement system would be a gigantic undertaking. The US switching to metric this late in the game would be by far the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

---

## 🧠 Cultural Resistance

Why hasn't America gone full-on metric? The simple answer is that the overwhelming majority of Americans have never wanted to. Whenever the discussion of switching unit systems arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and American citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle of changing the country's entire infrastructure. Many also believed that the United States should keep its particular system, setting it apart from other countries.

---

## ⚖️ Legal & Policy Failures

U.S. customary units have been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and according to United States law, the SI has been the "preferred system of weights and measures for United States trade and commerce" since 1975. The U.S. actually has a national policy to adopt the metric system. However, the 1975 Metric Conversion Act promoted metrication, but was not mandatory. It left adoption up to individual industries, and without legal compulsion, few sectors saw the benefit of making the switch.

---

## ✅ The US Is More Metric Than You Think

It's not a complete uphill battle. American manufacturers have put out all-metric cars, and the wine and spirits industry abandoned fifths for 750-milliliter bottles. The metric system is, quietly and behind the scenes, now the standard in most industries, with a few notable exceptions like construction. Many US industries heavily use the metric system, especially those with international ties or reliant on modern technology, including science, medicine, automotive, electronics, and manufacturing. Examples include pharmaceutical dosages in milligrams, automotive parts in millimeters, and consumer products with dual-labeled packaging.

---

## 📚 Potential Benefits

Globally adopting the metric system offers benefits like simplified international trade and communication, easier scientific collaboration, improved industrial efficiency, reduced errors, and streamlined education due to its coherent, decimal-based structure. Both US Customary and Metric are currently taught in schools, but students required to learn two measurement systems are more likely to be confused. One estimate suggests that a full conversion to a single measurement system could save roughly 71 days in the classroom and up to $17 billion.

---

**In summary**, switching to the metric system would be *extremely* hard — requiring massive financial investment, decades of transition time, sweeping changes to infrastructure, education, industry, and culture, and — most critically — the political will to make it mandatory. While the benefits are real, the sheer scale of the change and persistent public resistance have kept it from happening for over 200 years.
